title_zh: 把我从这个恶魔手里解放出来
subtitle_zh: 本期 Money Stuff，Matt Levine 与客座主持人 Mary Childs 聊了三件事。先是 Kalshi 把体育博彩包装成受 CFTC 监管的“互换（swap）”，借此绕开各州的博彩监管，如今闹到最高法院，而 Kalshi 自己或许反倒盼着被判不能做体育博彩、好从这桩“恶魔”生意里解脱出来。接着谈到 Goldman 股票部门如今靠主经纪商业务（prime brokerage）放贷赚的钱比靠交易中介还多，折射出大银行从自营交易转向为对冲基金和自营公司提供融资的趋势。最后是 Martin Shkreli 因做空并爆料制药股被 FTC 申请藐视法庭令，引出“做空到底算不算持有股票”的哲学争论。

turns.zh: 不知道，我们是该做。大家好，欢迎收听 Money Stuff 播客，这是我们每周聊跟钱有关的事的节目。我是 Matt Levine，为 Bloomberg Opinion 撰写 Money Stuff 专栏。

turns.en: I'm Mary Childs, the host of the new podcast, Mary in America, which is available wherever you get your podcasts.
turns.zh: 我是 Mary Childs，新播客 Mary in America 的主持人，你在任何听播客的平台都能找到它。

turns.en: And on YouTube. Okay, should we talk about sports betting?
turns.zh: YouTube 上也有。好，我们来聊聊体育博彩（sports betting）吧？

turns.en: We should.
turns.zh: 该聊聊。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: This is a live one.
turns.zh: 这可是个正热乎的话题。

turns.en: We talk about it a lot, but it just absolutely boggles my mind and the mind of everyone I talk to. It is now the official position of the U.S. government— that sports bets are federally regulated commodities derivatives. Or it was the position until about a week ago. It's complicated. So what happened is that like Calci, the prediction market, which like everything here is so like crazily path dependent. Calci is essentially in the business of like offering sports bets, right? Like it's essentially like that's the business model. But like it's so clear that no one involved in Calci wanted that. or sees that as the long-term vision. They're so clearly like embarrassed by it, right? Like they wanted to do prediction markets in the classic, like libertarian economist sense where it's like, we're going to have prediction markets on who will win the election and like what will happen in the economy and like what will happen to the wars. And like, it'll be a truth machine for the world to understand. And in order to have that work, you need to have like sort of uninformed retail customers for like the informed people to trade against. And it turns out that uninformed retail customers are we'll bet on the election, they'll bet on the Oscars, but what they really want to bet on is sports. And so, Kalshi has become largely a sports book.
turns.zh: 我们聊过很多次，但它真的让我和我聊过的所有人都匪夷所思。美国政府现在的官方立场是——体育博彩属于受联邦监管的商品衍生品（commodities derivatives）。或者说，直到大约一周前还是这个立场。这事很复杂。情况是这样的，Kalshi 这家预测市场（prediction market）公司——这里所有事都极其依赖路径、阴差阳错。Kalshi 本质上做的就是提供体育博彩，对吧？这基本就是它的商业模式。但很明显，Kalshi 里没人想要这样，也没人把这当成长期愿景。他们显然为此感到尴尬，对吧？他们想做的是经典意义上、那种自由意志主义经济学家所设想的预测市场，也就是：我们要就谁赢得大选、经济会怎样、战争会如何走向开设预测市场，让它成为一台让世界看清真相的“真理机器（truth machine）”。而要让这套运转起来，你需要有一批不太懂行的散户，好让懂行的人跟他们对手交易。结果发现，这些不懂行的散户会赌大选、会赌奥斯卡，但他们真正想赌的是体育。于是，Kalshi 在很大程度上变成了一家博彩公司（sports book）。

turns.en: Which we've heard of.
turns.zh: 这个我们听说过。

turns.en: Yeah. Because there's this history of like, oh, we should have prediction markets. Kalshi got itself legalized as a prediction market and fought the old Commodity Futures Trading Commission to allow it to list election contracts, which they won that case in court. And so, now they have this federally regulated prediction market, and they realized that listing sports bets is a good way to get people to come. And so they list mostly sports bets, and it's a big sports betting business. And most states have said, wait a minute, you're offering sports bets without following our sports betting regulation, including states where sports betting is illegal, right? You can't bet on sports in Utah, but you can on Cal State, right? And so there's this big push by many states to regulate Cal State, and Cal State has said, no, no, no. We are offering federally regulated swaps, and swaps are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. And because the CFTC regulates our sports bets, you can't, even though they're sports bets. And the CFTC has agreed with that and has filed briefs saying, yes, we are the exclusive regulator of these sports bets, and therefore states can't regulate them.
turns.zh: 是的。因为历史上一直有这种声音：哦，我们该搞预测市场。Kalshi 让自己拿到了预测市场的合法身份，还跟原来的 Commodity Futures Trading Commission（美国商品期货交易委员会，CFTC）打官司，争取让它上线大选合约，而且它在法庭上赢了这场官司。于是现在它有了这个受联邦监管的预测市场，然后他们发现，上线体育博彩是吸引用户的好办法。所以他们上线的大多是体育博彩，成了一大块体育博彩生意。而大多数州都说：等等，你在提供体育博彩，却不遵守我们的体育博彩监管，其中包括那些体育博彩违法的州，对吧？在 Utah 你不能赌体育，但在 Kalshi 上可以，对吧？于是很多州大力推动去监管 Kalshi，而 Kalshi 说：不不不，我们提供的是受联邦监管的互换（swap），而互换归 CFTC 专属管辖。因为 CFTC 监管我们的体育博彩，所以你们不能管——哪怕它们就是体育博彩。CFTC 也认同这一点，还提交了法庭文件说：是的，我们是这些体育博彩的唯一监管者，因此各州无权监管。

turns.en: And seems to be working to solidify that also.
turns.zh: 而且似乎还在努力巩固这一立场。

turns.en: Oh yeah. And it's been mixed results in courts. When I started writing about this, Kashi won most of these cases. Now it's more mixed and they've lost a couple of appeals cases. They've won an appeals case. And now the latest is that basically a state that lost and the appeals court has asked the Supreme court to review the case. And that's ongoing. Like their petition has been filed and surely the Supreme court will review it because there's a circuit split and it's a big deal. And I really, you know, I wrote this, I have no idea. how the Supreme Court will decide because there's good legal arguments both ways. But it's just like, as a policy matter, it's completely nuts. And there's so many things that are nuts about it. But the one I want to talk about is that one problem with this whole theory is that there's already been sports betting, right? And the reason that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction is because the bets on Cal State are swaps, which is very broadly defined in the statute to mean any contract whose payout is dependent on the Occurrence, non-occurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence. So the CFTC is like, look, sports have economic consequences, and so betting on a sports game is a swap, right? And what people realized, including the appeals courts that have found against Kalshi, was that what that would seem to imply is that all sports bets are swaps, not just the ones listed on Kalshi. And so what that means is that every state-regulated sportsbook is violating federal law because the way the swaps rules work is basically you can either have them listed on a regulated commodities exchange like Kalshi, or if you don't, you're not allowed to offer them to retail. So you can't sell swaps to retail investors except on a regulated exchange. So sportsbooks are not regulated exchanges. And so if you're offering sports bets to retail customers off Kalshi, you are apparently violating the law. And so this is like several courts ruled against Kelshi saying like, this is crazy. This can't be the rule, right? Like this is based on a, you know, 2010 change to the statute. And in 2010, no one was like, oh, this is going to make sportsbooks illegal, right? Like everyone understood that this did not apply to sportsbooks. Right. And so last week, realizing this problem and somewhat embarrassed by it, the CFTC put out like an emergency rule saying, no, no, sportsbooks are not swaps. That's okay. Like basically they said casino gambling style bets, including sports bets are not Swaps, and so they're not regulated by the CFTC. Only Kelsey's sports bets are regulated by the CFTC.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。法院那边的结果一直喜忧参半。我开始写这个话题时，Kalshi 大多数官司都赢。现在就更参差了，它输了几起上诉案，也赢了一起上诉案。而最新的进展基本上是：一个败诉的州在上诉法院那边，已经请求 Supreme Court（最高法院）复审这个案子。这事还在进行中，他们的复审申请已经提交，最高法院几乎肯定会受理，因为各巡回法院出现了分歧，而且这是件大事。我真的，你知道，我写这篇的时候，完全不知道最高法院会怎么判，因为两边的法律论点都站得住脚。但单纯从政策角度看，这完全疯了。里面有很多离谱的地方，但我想谈的那一点是：这整套理论的一个问题在于，体育博彩早就存在了，对吧？CFTC 之所以有专属管辖权，是因为 Kalshi 上的博彩属于互换，而法规里对互换的定义非常宽泛，指任何其赔付取决于某个事件或偶发情况是否发生、不发生、或发生程度的合约，且该事件带有潜在的金融、经济或商业后果。所以 CFTC 就说：看，体育有经济后果，因此赌一场体育比赛就是互换，对吧？而人们——包括那些判 Kalshi 败诉的上诉法院——意识到，这似乎意味着所有体育博彩都是互换，不只是 Kalshi 上线的那些。这样一来就意味着，每一家受州监管的博彩公司都在违反联邦法，因为互换规则的运作方式基本上是：你要么把它们放在像 Kalshi 这样受监管的商品交易所上市，要么就不能向散户提供。也就是说，除了受监管的交易所，你不能向散户投资者出售互换。而博彩公司不是受监管的交易所。所以如果你在 Kalshi 之外向散户提供体育博彩，你显然就违法了。于是有好几家法院判 Kalshi 败诉，说这太荒唐了，规则不可能是这样的，对吧？这是基于，你知道，2010 年对法规的一次修改。而在 2010 年，没人会说“哦，这会让博彩公司变非法”，对吧？大家都明白这不适用于博彩公司。于是上周，CFTC 意识到这个问题、也有点为此尴尬，就发布了一条紧急规则，说：不不，博彩公司的那些不是互换，那没问题。基本上他们说的是，赌场赌博式的投注（包括体育博彩）不是互换，因此不受 CFTC 监管。只有 Kalshi 的体育博彩才受 CFTC 监管。

turns.en: And those are very different.
turns.zh: 而这两者差别很大。

turns.en: You know, this is like people.
turns.zh: 你知道，这就像人们说的——

turns.en: They're so different.
turns.zh: 它们差别太大了。

turns.en: Look, there are differences.
turns.zh: 听着，确实有区别。

turns.en: I'm confused.
turns.zh: 我糊涂了。

turns.en: You can like resell. It's like, as a person interested in market structure, I don't find the differences that compelling, right? They're both binary bets on sports outcomes. You can bet on like the same things. You can bet like the point spread. You can bet like over, under. You can bet like same game parlays on how many touchdowns. You can do all of the sports bets, but because they're technically offered in a peer-to-peer marketplace and you can trade out of them rather than being offered on a one-to-many sports book, then they're different. They're different.
turns.zh: 你可以转卖。作为一个对市场结构（market structure）感兴趣的人，我觉得这些区别并不那么有说服力，对吧？它们都是对体育结果的二元投注。你能赌的东西是一样的。你可以赌让分盘（point spread），可以赌大小盘（over/under），可以赌同场串关（same-game parlay），赌会有多少次达阵。所有体育博彩你都能做，只不过因为它们从技术上是在一个点对点市场里提供、你可以把持仓平掉，而不是在一个一对多的博彩公司里提供，它们就“不一样”了。它们就不一样了。

turns.en: And there you have it.
turns.zh: 就是这么回事。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: It doesn't feel good. It doesn't feel clean in there. It feels messy.
turns.zh: 这感觉不好。这里面感觉不干净，乱糟糟的。

turns.en: It feels gross to me. Yeah. I don't know how to handicap this. My gut is that Kalshi is like the slight favorite in the Supreme Court. I've heard from others who follow this more closely that they disagree. And I think that Kalshi is the slight underdog. You know, there's all these like competing interests, right? Like on the one hand, this is nuts. On the other hand, like Kalshi's reading of the statute seems a little better. On the one hand, like the Supreme Court really likes the Trump administration and lets them do whatever they want. And like, this is something the Trump administration wants. On the other hand, the Supreme Court likes state rights and the states want something else. So I really don't know how it'll, how it'll go. But I wonder if Cal State would be like relieved if they were told you can't have sports bets, right?
turns.zh: 我也觉得很恶心。是的。我不知道该怎么评估这场官司。我的直觉是，Kalshi 在最高法院那边算是略被看好的一方。我也听一些跟得更紧的人说他们不同意，觉得 Kalshi 反而是略处下风的一方。你知道，这里有各种相互角力的因素，对吧？一方面，这很荒唐；另一方面，Kalshi 对法规的解读似乎更站得住脚一点。一方面，最高法院很喜欢 Trump 政府，让他们想干什么就干什么，而这正是 Trump 政府想要的；另一方面，最高法院又重视州权，而各州想要的是另一回事。所以我真不知道会怎么判。但我在想，如果 Kalshi 被告知不能做体育博彩，他们会不会反而松一口气，对吧？

turns.en: They're like, thank you. We're just a truth machine.
turns.zh: 他们会说：谢谢，我们只是一台真理机器。

turns.en: Yeah. On this podcast last week, we had on a guest, Jeremy Mallets, who's like a prediction markets trader at Susquehanna, who like definitely trades sports, you know, because that's what there is. But who like mostly wanted to talk about like companies hedging real economic risk, people wanting to hedge election risk, people wanting to hedge data center moratorium and credit risk. Like, Really big economic questions. And it is clearly the case that like in the prediction market ecosystem, that's what people want to talk about, right? They don't want to be like, oh yeah, we have parlays, right? Like now they have parlays, right? Like they have a lot of sports betting because that's where the money is. But like everyone is hunting bigger game or at least less embarrassing game.
turns.zh: 是的。上周我们这档播客请了一位嘉宾 Jeremy Mallets，他是 Susquehanna 的预测市场交易员，他当然也做体育交易，你知道，因为现在能赌的就是这些。但他更想聊的是企业如何对冲真实经济风险、人们想对冲大选风险、想对冲数据中心暂停令和信用风险，也就是真正重大的经济议题。而且很显然，在预测市场这个生态里，那才是大家想谈的，对吧？他们不想显得像是“哦对，我们有串关”，对吧？现在他们确实有串关，也有大量体育博彩，因为钱就在那儿。但每个人都在追更大的猎物，或者至少是没那么丢脸的猎物。

turns.en: Less embarrassing game because mentioned markets are also pretty big and not that intellectually satisfying.
turns.zh: 没那么丢脸的猎物，因为提及市场（mention market）也挺大，而且在智力上并不那么有意思。

turns.en: Well, I don't think mentioned markets are big. They get a lot of coverage. But I don't think that, like, Susquehanna is trading merchant markets. No, no.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不觉得提及市场很大。它们得到很多报道。但我不觉得，比如 Susquehanna 在交易提及市场。不，不。

turns.en: I don't think they're big in size. I think they're big in popularity.
turns.zh: 我不觉得它们规模大，我觉得它们是热度大。

turns.en: Right. And also embarrassing. And also, like, weirdly— Humiliating.
turns.zh: 对。而且还丢人。而且还，怎么说，莫名地——羞辱人。

turns.en: Insider trading.
turns.zh: 内幕交易（insider trading）。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. The CFTC has put out some, like, proposed rules about how it's going to regulate. They're like, wow. I think I've talked about them on this podcast. It's like, you're allowed to bet on college sports but not Little League on Calci. You know, it's like, it's great.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。CFTC 出了一些拟议规则，讲它打算怎么监管。那些规则简直了。我想我在这档播客里聊过。比如，在 Kalshi 上你可以赌大学体育，但不能赌少年棒球联盟（Little League）。你知道，这真是……太棒了。

turns.en: They're like, that's too far. It has to be professionals.
turns.zh: 他们会说：那就太过分了，必须是职业比赛才行。

turns.en: My reading of those rules is that they would crack down on mention markets. I don't know if that's right. It's all sort of qualitative. But my sense of those rules is that they want to avoid prediction markets, listing markets where like one person can just decide the outcome and mentioned markets are just obviously subject to manipulation in a way that like you're going to have bets on the outcome of a baseball game because there are a lot of people involved in that and it's hard to rig. Right. But Bets on whether a pitch will be a ball or a strike are famously easy to rig. And so in regular sports books, there are allegations of people rigging those. And so the CFTC wants to discourage those kinds of bets on prediction markets. I think mention markets are just exactly that, right? It's just like you bet on some guy saying something and then the guy says something and makes a hundred bucks, right? It's super embarrassing.
turns.zh: 我对这些规则的解读是，它们会打压提及市场。我不知道这对不对，反正都是定性的东西。但我对这些规则的感觉是，他们想避免预测市场上线那种一个人就能决定结果的市场，而提及市场显然极易被操纵；相比之下，你会赌一场棒球赛的结果，因为涉及的是一大批人，很难做手脚，对吧。但赌一个投球是坏球还是好球，是出了名的容易操纵。所以在常规博彩公司里，有人被指控操纵这类盘口。因此 CFTC 想在预测市场上抑制这类投注。我觉得提及市场就正是这一类，对吧？就是你赌某个人会说某句话，然后那人真说了，你就赚了一百块，对吧？太丢人了。

turns.en: Or his teleprompter.
turns.zh: 或者是他的提词器（teleprompter）。

turns.en: Yes, yes, yes.
turns.zh: 对，对，对。

turns.en: As happened to me, I was on Kalshi. We were doing an episode for Planet Money. I was working with Bobby Allen. And we traded in a mentioned market of a Trump speech about Iran. And I'm like pretty sure based on the time that this happened that I was trading against the informed teleprompter operator. I feel like I'm owed damages.
turns.zh: 我就碰上过，我当时在 Kalshi 上。我们在为 Planet Money 做一期节目，我合作的是 Bobby Allen。我们交易了一个提及市场，赌的是 Trump 一场关于 Iran 的演讲。根据发生的时间，我几乎可以肯定，我的对手盘就是那个消息灵通的提词器操作员。我觉得我该拿到赔偿。

turns.en: Right. Yeah. So Trump's teleprompter operator was like allegedly insider trading on mentioned markets on Cal State.
turns.zh: 对。是啊。所以说，Trump 的提词器操作员涉嫌在 Kalshi 的提及市场上做内幕交易。

turns.en: Against me.
turns.zh: 跟我对手交易。

turns.en: I do hope that you or Planet Money will. Yeah. Yeah. I think actually the prediction markets, they're really into enforcement on this stuff and they might actually refund your money.
turns.zh: 我真希望你或者 Planet Money 会去追讨。是的，是的。我觉得实际上，预测市场这方面对执法很上心，他们说不定真会把钱退给你。

turns.en: I will let you know.
turns.zh: 我会告诉你结果的。

turns.en: I don't know. That's not financial advice. Do let us know. I can't think of if there's been a case for victims of Calci Insider Trading demanding their money back. But should we move along?
turns.zh: 不知道。这不构成投资建议。一定要告诉我们。我想不出有没有过 Kalshi 内幕交易的受害者要求退钱的先例。不过我们是不是往下走？

turns.en: You don't want my pancakes or stuff?
turns.zh: 你不想听我讲松饼那些事吗？

turns.en: Oh, yeah. Do your pancakes.
turns.zh: 哦，想啊。讲讲你的松饼。

turns.en: To me, this whole... To me, whether... I'm so glad I'm able to bring this to the table, okay? So to speak. Okay. The question of Kalshi's sports bets and what jurisdiction they fall under and who gets to regulate them, it feels to me like the time I went to Waffle House in college when I really wanted a pancake. And I know, you and I both know, that waffles and pancakes are the same batter. And, or can be. And you don't know that?
turns.zh: 对我来说，这整件事……对我来说，是不是……我太高兴能把这个端上桌了，好吗？一语双关那种。好。Kalshi 的体育博彩归谁管辖、该由谁来监管这个问题，让我想起大学时我特别想吃松饼，就去了 Waffle House。我知道——你我都清楚——华夫饼和松饼用的是同一种面糊，或者说可以是同一种。你不知道吗？

turns.en: I'm not usually the maker of pancake or waffle batter in my house, but I do think that in my house, the pancake and waffle batter are distinctly different. I've ruined your story.
turns.zh: 在家里我通常不是那个调松饼或华夫饼面糊的人，但我确实觉得，在我家，松饼和华夫饼的面糊是明显不一样的。我把你的故事毁了。

turns.en: To me, it doesn't matter. or I don't know the taste difference. I'm not that deep of a connoisseur. So I went to Waffle House, but I wanted a pancake, but there were no pancake purveyors in my town. And so I said, could I please have a waffle, but I want it flat. And they're like, what? And I was like, can I have a waffle, but with no ridges? And they were like, That's a pancake. And I was like, no, no, no, no, no. It's a waffle. I just want to, I just today, I want, anyway, they would not do it. They would not give me, you could just pour it right on the griddle. You and I can both see in the Waffle House that it has a flat griddle right there. I don't get it. I don't know why they wouldn't do it, but it's like that. It's just like that.
turns.zh: 对我来说无所谓，或者说我吃不出味道差别，我不是那种很讲究的美食家。所以我去了 Waffle House，但我想要松饼，可我们镇上没有卖松饼的地方。于是我说，能不能给我来个华夫饼，但我要平的。他们说：啥？我说，能不能来个华夫饼，但不要那些格子纹。他们说：那就是松饼啊。我说：不不不不不，它是华夫饼，我今天就是想要……反正他们不肯做。他们不肯给我——你直接把面糊倒在煎板上不就行了。你我在 Waffle House 都能看到，那儿就摆着一块平底煎板。我搞不懂，不知道为什么他们不肯做，但事情就是这样，就是这么回事。

turns.en: It's just like that. You're assuming more knowledge of Waffle House than I actually have.
turns.zh: 就是这么回事。你高估了我对 Waffle House 的了解。

turns.en: You didn't actually need it. I gave you what you needed.
turns.zh: 其实你并不需要懂，我已经把你需要知道的都告诉你了。

turns.en: The fact that it was a griddle was the main thing. I don't know if I just have a good series of waffle presses.
turns.zh: 关键是那块平底煎板。不知道是不是只是因为我有一系列好用的华夫饼机。

turns.en: But it did also make me think of how lending used to be. Like, if you think about the why are we so obsessed with whether or not it's gambling? We regulate gambling. We don't like it as a society. But it is, if you think too hard about it, pretty confusing because the substance, the market structure, some of these things feel very similar. And it reminds me of the long history of credit and how that used to be illegal. It used to be very morally wrong under most religions, major religions to lend. and to get interest for your lending. And then we give up on that.
turns.zh: 但这确实也让我想起过去的借贷是怎样的。想想看，为什么我们这么执着于它到底算不算赌博？我们监管赌博，作为一个社会我们不喜欢赌博。但如果你认真去想，这其实挺让人困惑的，因为从实质、从市场结构看，这些东西感觉非常相似。这让我想起信贷漫长的历史，以及它过去曾经是非法的。在大多数宗教、主要宗教里，放贷、并因放贷收取利息，过去被认为在道德上非常错误。后来我们放弃了这个观念。

turns.en: One thing I think about, I read it this week, like clearly for hundreds of years, one thing you could do in the stock market was gamble, right? And clearly now you have a range of gambling type options in your brokerage account, in your legitimate brokerage account. Not even the sports bets, like not even crypto. You can trade options in a way that feels very gambling-like and gives you the same sort of like adrenaline rush and has the same like expectation of loss. And it's, you know, broadly speaking, like that's kind of like gambling, right?
turns.zh: 我这周读到一件事，也让我想到：显然几百年来，在股票市场里你能做的一件事就是赌博，对吧？而现在显然你的券商账户里、你那个正经的券商账户里，就有一系列赌博式的期权。甚至都不用说体育博彩，甚至都不用说加密货币。你可以用一种非常像赌博的方式交易期权（options），它给你带来同样的肾上腺素飙升，也有同样亏损的预期。而且，你知道，笼统地说，那其实就有点像赌博，对吧？

turns.en: Which is what Kalshi says. They're like, if we are gambling, then so is that.
turns.zh: 这正是 Kalshi 的说法。他们说：如果我们算赌博，那那个也算。

turns.en: Right. If you just sort of start from a place of we want to have like deep and liquid capital markets.
turns.zh: 对。如果你就是从“我们想要有深度、流动性充足的资本市场（capital markets）”这个前提出发。

turns.en: And we do.
turns.zh: 而我们确实想要。

turns.en: For retirement savers to invest their money and for companies to raise capital. And then you think about how would we get there? You'd be like, well, you'd have options market. And then like one thing leads to another. And like some people are speculating, right? Right. And it's like some retail investors are speculating. And you're like, well, yeah, that's the cost of having these deep and liquid capital markets. It's like, we can't stop people from speculating, but like, that's not the goal of the thing. The goal is something else, right? With sports betting, the goal is sports betting.
turns.zh: 让为退休存钱的人能投资他们的钱，让企业能融资。然后你再想，我们怎么做到这一点？你会说：嗯，那得有期权市场。接着一环扣一环，就会有人投机，对吧。会有一些散户在投机。你会说：嗯，是啊，这就是拥有这些深度、流动性充足资本市场的代价。我们没法阻止人们投机，但那不是这件事的目标，目标是别的东西，对吧？而体育博彩，目标就是体育博彩本身。

turns.en: But like, where does it stop? It doesn't make any, it stops making sense.
turns.zh: 但到底在哪儿是个头？这讲不通，它开始讲不通了。

turns.en: It doesn't stop. And again, with Calci, like they would say, no, our goal is to have deep and liquid and informative prediction markets that allow one, Truth machines, we know who will win the election, blah, blah, blah. And two, companies to hedge the legitimate economic risk of like a bar not selling enough beer, but also like, you know, data centers get a shutdown or whatever, right? It's like real huge economic risks and also fake sports related economic risks. And Kashi would say, look, if we're going to have that, like the sports, which are, you know, most of the businesses, The sports are, like, an epiphenomenon on that, but, like, you can't throw out the baby with the bathwater, and you have to, like, allow a certain amount of sports gambling to get the, like, deep and liquid hedging markets that you want.
turns.zh: 没有尽头。再说 Kalshi，他们会说：不，我们的目标是拥有深度、流动性充足、能提供信息的预测市场，一来实现真理机器，让我们知道谁会赢得大选，等等等等；二来让企业能对冲正当的经济风险，比如一家酒吧啤酒卖得不够多，又比如数据中心被关停之类，对吧？这些是真实而巨大的经济风险，也有那些虚假的、跟体育相关的经济风险。Kalshi 会说：看，如果我们要实现那个目标，体育虽然是业务的大头，但体育只是这上面的一个附带现象，你不能把婴儿和洗澡水一起倒掉，你得允许一定程度的体育赌博，才能得到你想要的那种深度、流动性充足的对冲市场。

turns.en: Come for the sports betting, stay to truth machine?
turns.zh: 为体育博彩而来，为真理机器而留？

turns.en: There's, like, a touch of truth to that argument. Like, I don't think that's a crazy argument. It's just, like, it looks bad. I don't know.
turns.zh: 这个说法有那么一点道理。我不觉得这是个荒唐的论点，只是……它看起来不太好看。我不知道。

turns.en: I don't know. Is that right? I don't think it's right, but it's nice.
turns.zh: 我不知道。这说得对吗？我不觉得对，但听着挺美。

turns.en: No, I think there is some truth to it in that, like, Traditionally, people would say prediction markets are like a dead end because no one wants to come and spend all day gambling on elections because there's just not that many elections.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得它有一定道理，因为传统上人们会说预测市场像是条死路，因为没人愿意整天来赌大选，毕竟大选本来就没几次。

turns.en: Yeah, you run out pretty fast.
turns.zh: 是啊，很快就赌完了。

turns.en: I think that some of the theory here is that if you have a site that is liquid every day, that people come to every day, then you'll have professional market makers. people will get into the business of being good at those predictions because there's money to be made there. And then that will make the truth machines good and it'll make the hedging, you know, there's something to that.
turns.zh: 我觉得这里的部分理论是：如果你有一个每天都有流动性、人们每天都来的网站，那你就会有专业的做市商（market maker）。会有人专门去把预测做准、把这当成一门生意，因为那里有钱可赚。这样一来，真理机器就会好用，对冲也会好用，你知道，这说法有点道理。

turns.en: And it allows the business to function because it's making money from the sports.
turns.zh: 而且它让这门生意能运转起来，因为钱是从体育那边赚来的。

turns.en: Right, right, right, right. So I think there's some, some reality to that, but it is just super weird to be like, we're not doing sports gambling. We're doing something completely different. It's swaps, swaps on how many touchdowns Joe Burrow.
turns.zh: 对对对对。所以我觉得这里面有一些现实依据，但说什么“我们不是在做体育赌博，我们做的是完全不同的东西，是互换，是赌 Joe Burrow 会有多少次达阵的互换”，这也太怪了。

turns.en: I can't wait for more clarity here. I've stayed confused on this.
turns.zh: 我盼着这事儿能更清楚点。我一直被它搞得很糊涂。

turns.en: Yeah. You know, the Supreme Court has to decide it. I'm sure it'll be weird. Maybe they'll say, Kashi can't lift sports contracts. And then Kashi will have spent so much time. No, maybe it'll be great. Maybe like they'll have grown their business so much and they'll be like mostly hedging data center risk. And they'll be like, it's okay. We didn't need the sports gambling. That was just like bootstrapping us to the glorious place we're at today.
turns.zh: 是啊。你知道，最高法院得来做裁决。我敢说结果会很奇怪。也许他们会说，Kalshi 不能上线体育合约，那 Kalshi 就白花了那么多功夫。不，也许结果会很好。也许他们会把业务做得很大，主要在对冲数据中心风险，然后他们会说：没关系，我们本来就不需要体育赌博，那只是把我们一路托举到今天这个辉煌位置的垫脚石。

turns.en: It's like when a kid really needs a parent to make them stop doing something. They're like, please release me from this demon. That's what the Supreme Court can do for Kelshi.
turns.zh: 这就像一个孩子真的很需要父母来阻止自己做某件事，他会说：请把我从这个恶魔手里解放出来。这正是最高法院能为 Kalshi 做的事。

turns.en: I don't want to speculate about their psychology.
turns.zh: 我不想揣测他们的心理。

turns.en: But you're going to do it.
turns.zh: 但你会揣测的。

turns.en: But I feel like part of them, they'd be a little pleased to be released from the demon of sports betting. They're not here to be sports books.
turns.zh: 但我觉得他们心里有一部分，会为能从体育博彩这个恶魔手里解脱出来而有点高兴。他们来这儿不是为了当博彩公司的。

turns.en: We all just want boundaries, you know? We just want boundaries and we want to know where they are.
turns.zh: 我们都只是想要界限，你懂吧？我们只是想要界限，还想知道界限在哪儿。

turns.en: There is a lot of money in sports betting, so I don't know.
turns.zh: 体育博彩里有很多钱，所以我不好说。

turns.en: Speaking of a lot of money.
turns.zh: 说到很多钱。

turns.en: Always a good transition on the Money Slip Podcast.
turns.zh: 在 Money Stuff 播客上，这永远是个好用的转场。

turns.en: Matt, we're banks making money now.
turns.zh: Matt，银行现在赚钱吗？

turns.en: All sorts of places. AI financing. But there's a good Bloomberg story this week about Goldman's equities division. I was going to say disclosure where I once worked, but that's not true. I worked in equity capital markets, which is not part of the equities division, but it doesn't matter.
turns.zh: 各种地方都在赚，AI 融资就是。不过这周 Bloomberg 有一篇很好的报道，讲的是 Goldman 的股票部门。我本来想做个利益披露说我曾在那儿工作，但其实不是。我当时在股权资本市场（equity capital markets）部门，那不属于股票部门，不过这也不重要。

turns.en: And derivatives.
turns.zh: 还有衍生品（derivatives）。

turns.en: Yeah. Some of my revenue fed up to the equities division. Anyway, Goldman's equities division, they have two businesses. They have intermediation and they have prime brokerage or financing, right? So they have the business of financing stock positions and they have the business of actually trading stocks. They made more money on prime brokerage on financing than they did on intermediation. So this is like a trend that I've written about a few times where it used to be that prime brokerage was like kind of like a little sideline of like these big trading businesses that made most of their money by taking trading risk. And now it's like increasingly a big part of the business. And instead of like taking a lot of position risk on stocks and bonds and derivatives, these big banks are now instead lending a lot of money to hedge funds and prop trading firms that are doing the trading, which I think is an interesting shift.
turns.zh: 是的。我的一部分收入最后归到了股票部门。总之，Goldman 的股票部门有两块业务：一块是中介业务（intermediation），另一块是主经纪商业务（prime brokerage），也就是融资。所以他们既有为股票持仓提供融资的业务，也有实际交易股票的业务。他们在主经纪商、在融资上赚的钱，比在中介业务上赚的还多。这是我写过几次的一个趋势：过去主经纪商业务有点像这些大型交易业务的小副业，那些业务主要靠承担交易风险赚钱；而现在它越来越成为业务的一大块。这些大银行不再对股票、债券和衍生品承担大量头寸风险，而是转而把大量资金借给真正在做交易的对冲基金和自营交易公司，我觉得这是个有意思的转变。

turns.en: I was trying to puzzle through like, banking was very relationship-based. And then you went into banks did a lot of trading, which was skill in trading, that kind of actual mechanical. It was more commodified and talent-based in the market. And then now Prime feels very relationship-motivated and the people who are the best at it often are the best at cultivating and maintaining relationships. It just seems like it's sort of going back in a way.
turns.zh: 我在琢磨这么件事：银行业过去非常靠关系。后来银行做了大量交易，那靠的是交易的技巧、那种实际的机械能力，在市场上更被商品化、更靠天赋。而现在主经纪商业务感觉又非常靠关系驱动，最擅长这块的人往往就是最擅长培养和维护关系的人。看起来在某种意义上又绕回去了。

turns.en: Yeah, it is. I mean, one thing that's happening is that Trading is probably less relationship-based than it used to be. Usually bond trading was like- That's what I mean, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。我的意思是，正在发生的一件事是，交易可能不像以前那样靠关系了。过去债券交易通常是那样——我就是这个意思，是的。

turns.en: Way back.
turns.zh: 很久以前的事了。

turns.en: You would take the customers out for drinks, and then they'd be like, oh, we'll call that guy. We need to buy bonds. And you'd pay a quarter point to buy the bonds, right? But now a lot of trading.
turns.zh: 你会请客户出去喝酒，然后他们会说：哦，我们打给那个人吧，我们要买债券。于是你会多付四分之一个点去买这些债券，对吧？但现在很多交易……

turns.en: Is on screen, and- You don't really need a person.
turns.zh: 都在屏幕上完成了，而且——你其实不需要一个真人。

turns.en: The bank's relationships are less important, and so it's easier for the Jane Streets and Citadel Securities of the world to do that business. And by the way, those firms are also like building up relationships, right? So a lot more trading intermediation is being done by prop market-making firms and also a little bit of a hedge funds. And meanwhile, those firms are like so big and institutional and so like risk managed that they need a lot of financing and they can get a lot of financing. They can go to a bank and say like, we need 10 times leverage on our positions. And the bank will be like, that's pretty safe because, like, you're a pretty, like, you know, well-risk managed firm, so it'll give them a lot of leverage. And that's a relationship business, right? Like, that's, like, the bank has a very close and commercially important relationship with, like, the big prop trading firms and the big hedge funds. And so, yeah, they're lending them a lot of money and they're making their money on lending rather than trading.
turns.zh: 银行的关系就没那么重要了，于是世界上那些 Jane Street、Citadel Securities 之类的公司就更容易做这块业务。顺便说一句，这些公司也在建立关系，对吧？所以越来越多的交易中介业务是由自营做市公司来做的，也有一部分由对冲基金做。与此同时，这些公司规模庞大、非常机构化、风险管理又做得极好，以至于他们需要大量融资、也能拿到大量融资。他们可以去跟银行说：我们的头寸需要 10 倍杠杆。银行会说：这挺安全的，因为你是个风险管理很好的公司，于是就会给他们很高的杠杆。而这门生意是靠关系的，对吧？银行跟那些大型自营交易公司、大型对冲基金有着非常紧密、商业上非常重要的关系。所以，是的，银行把钱大量借给他们，靠放贷而不是靠交易赚钱。

turns.en: And the job becomes protecting that relationship and making sure they're happy.
turns.zh: 于是这份工作就变成了维护那段关系、确保他们满意。

turns.en: Well, to be clear, the job is also protecting the credit risk, right?
turns.zh: 嗯，说清楚点，这份工作也包括把控信用风险（credit risk），对吧？

turns.en: There are ways it can go wrong.
turns.zh: 它有很多方式会出问题。

turns.en: Yeah, like... In the business of intermediation, right? Like one thing you're doing is you're trying to get your clients to like you so that they call you to do trades. But another thing you're doing is you're trying not to get run over, right? You're trying not to buy bonds that are going down or whatever, hold stocks too long while they go down.
turns.zh: 是的，比如……在中介业务里，对吧？你做的事情之一是让客户喜欢你，好让他们打电话找你做交易。但你做的另一件事是尽量别被碾压，对吧？你要尽量别买那些正在下跌的债券之类的，或者在股票下跌时持有太久。

turns.en: You don't want to be their stupid friend. Yeah.
turns.zh: 你不想当他们那个傻乎乎的朋友。是的。

turns.en: Yeah. And in prime brokerage, same thing, right? With like slightly different like parameters, right? Like you really want to lend billions of dollars to the situational awareness because- They want leverage and they're making a lot of money and they're paying you a lot of money. I think, you know, Goldman was one of the banks for situational awareness. And I think there are stories about how the banks made a lot of money providing financing to situational awareness before it had a bit of an oopsie this year. But if you are their bank, you really also want to make sure that you're not left holding a bag when they have an oopsie. The old trading business is like, partly you're just like clipping fees and partly you're taking a lot of market risk, right? Because like, At any moment, you own a lot of stocks and bonds. And if, you know, if they go down, you lose money. Right. Or you're short a lot of, you know, and then they go up, you lose money. The prime brokerage business is similarly a business where you earn like steady fees by charging interest, but a business where if the stuff you're financing goes down, then, you know, you send it a margin call and it's fine.
turns.zh: 是的。在主经纪商业务里也一样，对吧？只是参数略有不同。比如你确实想把数十亿美元借给 Situational Awareness，因为——他们想要杠杆，他们在赚大钱，也在付给你很多钱。我想，你知道，Goldman 是 Situational Awareness 的贷款银行之一。而且我想有报道说，在今年它出了一次小翻车之前，各家银行靠给 Situational Awareness 提供融资赚了不少钱。但如果你是他们的银行，你还真得确保在他们翻车时，别让自己接盘被套。旧的交易业务是这样的：一部分你只是在赚取费用，另一部分你在承担大量市场风险，对吧？因为任何时候你都持有大量股票和债券，如果它们下跌，你就亏钱，对吧；或者你做空了很多，然后它们上涨，你也亏钱。主经纪商业务同样是一门你靠收利息赚取稳定费用的生意，但也是一门——如果你融资的对象下跌了，你就发一份追加保证金通知（margin call），那就没事——的生意。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But if it goes down more, then you lose a lot of money. All right. So there are certainly cases of, you know, Archegos is the big one recently, but there are others. of like prime brokers.
turns.zh: 但如果它跌得更多，你就会亏很多钱。好了。所以确实有这样的案例，你知道，Archegos 是最近最大的一个，但还有别的，都是主经纪商的案例。

turns.en: Recently.
turns.zh: 最近。

turns.en: People just, it's not that, I know I'm so old. It's okay. It's like 20 years ago. But like, you know, prime brokers like losing their shirts, financing positions that go down. And that's definitely a risk, but it's like, you know, one thing I've written about a lot is like banking has gotten like narrower and safer. And like, Yeah. One aspect of that is like, you know, so like instead of like making loans to like risky LBOs, now private credit firms make loans to risky LBOs and banks are provide like back leverage to the private credit firms so it's still the same like their money is still going to the same place.
turns.zh: 人们只是——不是说，我知道我太老了。没关系。那大概是 20 年前的事了。但你知道，主经纪商因为给下跌的头寸提供融资而亏得血本无归。那绝对是一种风险，但就像我写过很多次的：银行业变得更窄、更安全了。是的。其中一个方面是，你知道，过去银行给高风险的杠杆收购（LBO）放贷，现在是私募信贷公司给高风险的 LBO 放贷，而银行为私募信贷公司提供后端杠杆，所以其实是一样的，他们的钱还是流向了同一个地方。

turns.en: But you just added a degree of separation yeah they've added.
turns.zh: 但你们只是加了一层隔离，是的，他们加了。

turns.en: A degree of like seniority right so similarly here like banks don't do prop trading anymore but like they don't exactly own a concentrated book of ai stocks but they own you know half of that book right like they have like if that book goes down too much they lose their money so They're moving to a safer part of the capital structure, but they're still like involved in the same trades.
turns.zh: 加了一层优先级（seniority），对吧。所以这里也类似：银行不再做自营交易了，但他们并不是完全不持有一本集中的 AI 股票账簿，而是持有，你知道，那本账簿的一半，对吧？如果那本账簿跌得太多，他们就会亏钱。所以他们是在往资本结构（capital structure）里更安全的一层移动，但他们仍然参与着同样的交易。

turns.en: I like that because it's a little bit, everyone likes to wring their hands about private credit being riskier because we can't see it. I have done my share of hand wringing.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个说法，因为有点……大家都喜欢为私募信贷因为看不见而更危险这件事捶胸顿足。我自己也捶过不少。

turns.en: I don't wring hands.
turns.zh: 我不捶胸顿足。

turns.en: You don't wring hands. I see on the table, your hands are very far apart, unwrung.
turns.zh: 你不捶。我看到你的手放在桌上，两只手离得很开，没有捶。

turns.en: That's my best quality. I don't wring my hands. Never.
turns.zh: 这是我最好的品质。我不捶胸顿足，从来不。

turns.en: But I think that like, it's nice to consider the structure of it and to, I don't know, for once take solace in the. Perhaps it's an improvement.
turns.zh: 但我觉得，能好好想想它的结构、难得地从中得到一点安慰，是件好事。也许这是一种改进。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Like we're allowed to make improvements.
turns.zh: 就像我们是被允许做出改进的。

turns.en: This is like a general thing, I think, right? Like one thing that happened is that there was like a bank crisis in 2008. And then we're going to make the bank safer. And then like that had its intended effect. And so banks got out of some risky economic activity. And other people did the risky economic activity because there was still demand for it. And those other people have much better funding models than the banks, right? They have long-term locked-up funding from risk-seeking investors. They should be doing the risky activities. The problem with a banking crisis is that you're doing, you know, risky activities with deposits. And if you stop doing that and do risky activities with risk-seeking money, and also you get a little bit of leverage from banks, that's like strictly an improvement. But everyone's like, oh no, the banks are still lending money. So people still get mad about it because they're like, we just pushed the risk elsewhere in the system.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是个普遍现象，对吧？发生过的一件事是，2008 年有一场银行危机。然后我们要让银行更安全，而这确实达到了预期效果。于是银行退出了一些有风险的经济活动，而其他人在做这些有风险的经济活动，因为对它仍有需求。而这些其他人拥有比银行好得多的融资模式，对吧？他们有来自追求风险的投资者的长期锁定资金，本就该由他们来做这些有风险的活动。银行危机的问题在于，你是用存款去做有风险的活动。如果你不再那样做，而是用追求风险的钱去做风险活动，同时再从银行那里拿一点杠杆，那严格来说就是一种改进。但大家都说：哦不，银行还是在放贷。所以人们仍然为此生气，因为他们觉得：我们只是把风险推到了系统里的别处。

turns.en: I don't like risk.
turns.zh: 我不喜欢风险。

turns.en: Yes, you've pushed the risk to the less risky funding model. So it's fine. Anyway, by the way, I don't know if that's true here. Like that's like a general story about private credit. Here, like the funding models of like, The prop trading firms and hedge funds are, you know, they have like a lot of like locked up long-term funding because like they're managing either like very long-term locked up LPs money or like in the case of the prop trading firms, like their own money. But they also have a lot of leverage and yeah, there's ways for that to go wrong, but still, still.
turns.zh: 是的，你把风险推给了那个风险更小的融资模式，所以没问题。不过话说回来，我不知道这里是不是也这样，那只是关于私募信贷的一个笼统说法。在这里，自营交易公司和对冲基金的融资模式是，你知道，他们有大量长期锁定的资金，因为他们管理的要么是锁定期很长的 LP（有限合伙人）资金，要么——就自营交易公司而言——是他们自己的钱。但他们也有很高的杠杆，所以是的，这也可能出问题，但仍然，仍然算好一些。

turns.en: Tell us the story of Martin Shkreli.
turns.zh: 给我们讲讲 Martin Shkreli 的故事吧。

turns.en: Do people remember Martin Shkreli?
turns.zh: 大家还记得 Martin Shkreli 吗？

turns.en: People remember like a cartoon, but the reality is so much better. Martin Shkreli did.
turns.zh: 大家记得的是个漫画式的形象，但现实精彩多了。Martin Shkreli 做了……

turns.en: So many different things at the same time.
turns.zh: ……同时做了那么多不同的事。

turns.en: He's done it all, really.
turns.zh: 他真的什么都干过。

turns.en: Everyone got annoyed with him for sort of the whole complex of the things, but like legally you have to separate them, right? So here are some things he did. One is he like owned some drug companies, and to simplify, and I'm sure he would object to this, jacked up the prices of some drugs to make a lot of money for himself in ways that people really didn't like. So that's one thing he did. Another thing he did is that he ran some hedge funds that did some fairly basic fraud where he would raise money from investors and then yeet it all into options and lose it all and lie to them or whatever.
turns.zh: 大家都因为他这一整堆事情而讨厌他，但从法律上你得把它们分开看，对吧？这里是他做过的一些事。一件是，他拥有几家制药公司，简单说——我敢肯定他会反对这个说法——他哄抬了一些药品的价格，用大家非常反感的方式为自己赚了很多钱。这是他做的一件事。另一件是，他经营过几家对冲基金，做了相当基础的欺诈：他从投资者那里募资，然后把钱一股脑砸进期权，全亏光，再对他们撒谎之类的。

turns.en: Not good.
turns.zh: 这可不好。

turns.en: And then a third thing he did was that he bought this one-of-a-kind wu-tang clan album and was very annoying about that too he did some others oh and also he's terrible on twitter like really like obnoxious and like made threats and like.
turns.zh: 然后他做的第三件事，是买下了那张独一无二的 Wu-Tang Clan 专辑，而且为这事也很招人烦。他还做过别的——哦对，他在 Twitter 上也很糟糕，真的很讨人厌，还发出威胁之类的。

turns.en: Everything canonical troll yeah.
turns.zh: 样样齐全，一个标准的喷子，是的。

turns.en: So he did all those things and there were like legal comeuppance for all of them separately so he was charged with securities fraud for the hedge fund stuff which by the way it's like an incredible story he like lost all these investors money he rolled it into a new hedge fund lost all their money again and then he rolled like their equity interests into like his pharma company, which returned like a thousand times and like gave them all their money back. But he nonetheless went to prison for securities fraud because one, he did securities fraud and two, everyone hated him. Like he was so annoying.
turns.zh: 所以他做了所有这些事，而每一件都分别遭到了法律上的报应。他因为对冲基金那摊事被控证券欺诈（securities fraud）——顺便说一句，那是个难以置信的故事：他亏光了这些投资者的钱，把钱滚进一家新的对冲基金，又亏光了他们的钱，然后把他们的股权权益滚进了他的制药公司，而那家公司回报了大约一千倍，等于把他们的钱都还了回来。但他仍然因证券欺诈进了监狱，因为一来他确实犯了证券欺诈，二来所有人都恨他，他太招人烦了。

turns.en: Right, right. We're going to get you for something.
turns.zh: 对对。我们总得因点什么把你办了。

turns.en: Yeah. He like tweeted threats about people. Like it was like, he did not make a good case for himself in his trial. And so he went to prison for securities fraud. Separately, the drug stuff, jacking up the prices of the drugs. Eventually he got done for like anti-competitive conduct by like the Federal Trade Commission.
turns.zh: 是的。他在 Twitter 上对人发出威胁。就是说，他在自己的庭审里没给自己营造出什么好形象。所以他因证券欺诈进了监狱。另一码事是药品那摊——哄抬药价。最终他因为反竞争行为（anti-competitive conduct）被 Federal Trade Commission（联邦贸易委员会，FTC）办了。

turns.en: And- He got done.
turns.zh: 而且——他被办了。

turns.en: So- That was totally separate. There was a trial on that where his pharmaceutical company was charged with anti-competitive practices. He was in prison, I think, during this trial for the securities fraud stuff, which was separate. And the judge hated him because he was obnoxious. And the conclusion of the trial was basically he and his pharma company had to pay a big fine. And he was banned from the pharmaceutical industry for life in this incredibly broad way that included he was not allowed to acquire or hold any pharmaceutical stocks. And he wasn't allowed to take any action to directly or indirectly influence or control the management or business of any pharmaceutical company. And he said, well, that would infringe on my free speech rights to tweet about pharmaceuticals. And the judge was like, yes, do not tweet about pharmaceuticals.
turns.zh: 所以——那是完全独立的两码事。为此有一场庭审，他的制药公司被控反竞争行为。我记得在这场庭审期间，他正因为证券欺诈那件独立的事在坐牢。而法官讨厌他，因为他很讨人厌。这场庭审的结果基本上是：他和他的制药公司必须支付一大笔罚款，并且他被以一种极其宽泛的方式终身禁入制药行业，其中包括不允许他获取或持有任何制药类股票，也不允许他采取任何直接或间接的行动去影响或控制任何一家制药公司的管理或业务。他说：嗯，那会侵犯我就制药话题发推的言论自由权利。法官就说：是的，那就别就制药话题发推。

turns.en: Literally, that's what I'm going for.
turns.zh: 字面意思上，我就是这个意思。

turns.en: So she can't quite do that. But what she did was say, you can't tweet about them if a reasonable person would think that you're trying to influence pharmaceuticals. the management or control of them, which is pretty broad. And this was like upheld on appeal because everyone was really annoyed with him. And so he's gotten out of prison and he's been day trading pharmaceutical stocks and tweeting about it for a long time. And this week, the Federal Trade Commission and like seven or eight states filed for a contempt order, basically going back to court and saying he is not following the order in from his last trial. So you should, you should make him stop.
turns.zh: 所以她其实不能完全那样做。但她做的是说：如果一个理性的人会认为你在试图影响制药公司的管理或控制权，你就不能就它们发推——这范围相当宽。而且在上诉时这被维持了下来，因为大家都真的很烦他。所以他出狱后，很长一段时间一直在做制药股票的日内交易（day trading），并为此发推。这周，FTC 和大概七八个州申请了一道藐视法庭令，基本上是回到法庭说：他没有遵守上次庭审的裁定，所以你们应该让他停下来。

turns.en: He's still being annoying. Please stop him.
turns.zh: 他还是很招人烦。请让他停下来。

turns.en: There are several interesting.
turns.zh: 这里有好几个有意思的……

turns.en: Things about this.
turns.zh: ……地方。

turns.en: One thing that I think is slightly interesting is that the Federal Trade Commission, the actual commission, like the people in charge of the Federal Trade Commission, they voted to file this contempt order. And the vote was one to zero. Because the way that regulation works in the Trump administration is like, they fire all the Democratic commissioners, they don't replace them. And then like, Everyone is like somehow connected to the industry. So like there's two FTC commissioners and the chair had to recuse himself from this case. So there's one guy left.
turns.zh: 我觉得稍微有意思的一点是，FTC——也就是真正的那个委员会、那些主管 FTC 的人——他们投票决定提交这道藐视法庭令，而投票结果是一比零。因为在 Trump 政府下监管的运作方式是这样的：他们把所有民主党籍的委员都解职，又不补上。然后，大家又都多多少少跟这个行业有瓜葛。所以 FTC 只有两名委员，而主席在这个案子里必须回避，于是只剩下一个人。

turns.en: So there you have it.
turns.zh: 就是这么回事。

turns.en: And so he voted. Nonetheless, that one guy was like, yeah, Martin Shkreli, really annoying. They went to the court to be like, he's in contempt. He's of course tweeting like, I would expect this from totalitarians like Letitia James, but not from the Trump FTC. He really tweeted that.
turns.zh: 于是他投了票。尽管如此，那唯一的一个人是说：是啊，Martin Shkreli，真招人烦。他们就去法庭说他藐视法庭。他当然发推说：我料到像 Letitia James 这样的极权主义者会这么干，但没想到 Trump 的 FTC 也会。他真的发了这条推。

turns.en: Oh, our guy.
turns.zh: 哦，真是我们的人。

turns.en: The case is wild because like, I understand why people find him annoying, but like what happened here? is that he did some anti-competitive practices in the pharmaceutical industry. And to prevent that from happening again, they issued a broad order saying he can't try to influence the management of any pharmaceutical companies. I don't think he was trying to influence the management of any pharmaceutical companies. I think he was being a.
turns.zh: 这个案子很离谱，因为我理解大家为什么觉得他烦，但这里发生的事是：他在制药行业做了一些反竞争行为，而为了防止这类事再发生，他们发布了一道宽泛的命令，说他不能试图影响任何制药公司的管理。我不觉得他在试图影响任何制药公司的管理，我觉得他只是在当一个……

turns.en: Troll on Twitter. But he's a true influencer.
turns.zh: ……Twitter 上的喷子。但他是个真正有影响力的人。

turns.en: Yeah, okay. But like.
turns.zh: 是啊，好吧。但是……

turns.en: He's a true influencer. People follow him. People care what he says for better or worse. I guess that's right. And that is, his speech is influential. His speech is literally influential. What do you do about that?
turns.zh: 他是个真正有影响力的人。有人关注他，不管好坏，人们在乎他说什么。我想这没错。也就是说，他的言论是有影响力的，他的言论实实在在地有影响力。对此你能怎么办？

turns.en: I wonder if what happened here is that like the lawyers who worked on this case for like the states and the FTC are like, oh, this guy is annoying. Or if what happened here is that the pharmaceutical companies that he was criticizing were We're like, hey, he's not allowed to criticize me. And went to the FTC. It's possible it was that.
turns.zh: 我在想，这里发生的事，是不是那些为各州和 FTC 办这个案子的律师觉得：哦，这家伙真烦人。还是说，是他批评的那些制药公司觉得：嘿，他不许批评我，然后去找了 FTC。有可能是后者。

turns.en: I got this guy on my heels. Yeah.
turns.zh: 就是“这家伙紧咬着我不放”。是的。

turns.en: It's possible that they were like, oh my God, I'm going to have to change my whole strategy. I'm going to have to withdraw this drug from the market because he's being so mean about this drug I have. I don't know if that's the case.
